references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus asks the same question about what the people went out to see, and confirms that John was more than a prophet.
The people regarded John as a prophet, which confirms Jesus' words that John was a prophet and more than a prophet.
The people counted John as a prophet, which supports Jesus' statement that he was more than a prophet.
Zechariah prophesies over his son John and calls him 'the Prophet of the Most High', which aligns with Jesus' words that John was a prophet and more than a prophet.
The preceding verses in the same pericope where Jesus asks the people what they went out into the wilderness to see – the context for the question about the prophet.
The verse that follows immediately, where Jesus explains why John is more than a prophet by quoting Malachi 3:1 and declaring that no one born of women is greater than John.
The people were convinced that John was a prophet – this confirms the widespread view of John as a prophet.
Malachi prophesies about a messenger who will prepare the way, a prophecy Jesus applies to John the Baptist, which explains why John is 'more than a prophet'.
The prophecy that Elijah must come before the Lord's day. Jesus identifies John as the fulfillment of this prophecy, making him more than an ordinary prophet.
John himself denies being the Christ or Elijah, but identifies himself as a voice in the wilderness – he points beyond his role as a prophet to his unique mission as the forerunner of the Messiah.
